title: Holi: the colors of Braj
hookLine: the morning after the fire: Krishna, Radha, a handful of color, and lila, God at play
carry: lila: god plays, and love plays back
last: HOLI: THE FIRE THE NIGHT BEFORE.

cards: The fire has burned down to ash. Some people carry a little of it home, still warm, and touch it to their foreheads. The next morning, the street belongs to color.
Pink, green, yellow, a purple that won't wash out until Thursday. But why color? Nothing in Prahlada's story is pink.
For the colors, people tell a different, smaller story, set in a village by a river, about a boy who was worried about his skin. And that story tells you how to play Holi well.

teach.h: A DARK BOY WORRIED ABOUT HIS SKIN.
teach.b: The boy is Krishna, growing up among cowherds in Braj, the country around Mathura and Vrindavan. He's dark; the old poems call his skin the color of a rain cloud.
The story people tell is that he goes to his foster mother, Yashoda, upset: why is Radha so fair, and I'm so dark?

teach.h: GO AND COLOR HER FACE, THEN.
teach.b: Yashoda laughs: go and put some color on her face, then. So he does, and Radha and her friends put color right back on him. It's a story families and songs tell, not a scene from an old scripture.
But it carries one of Hinduism's big ideas: lila, God's play. In Braj, Krishna isn't a distant king. He's the Lord, and he plays: he steals butter, he dances, he throws color.
And in Braj devotion, Radha is the greatest of his devotees, so close in love that the color goes both ways. Holi lets everyone join the game.
In Barsana, Radha's village in the stories, women playfully chase the men from Krishna's village with long sticks, and the men hide behind shields and laugh.
In Vrindavan, some temples throw flower petals instead of powder.
Many people read the morning this way: for a few hours, everyone is the same messy color, old and young, boss and worker, and the distance between people drops. So the manners matter.
You start with elders: a pinch of gulal, the soft powder, on their feet, and a bow. You say happy Holi first, and you don't color anyone who's said no.

teach.h: GOD PLAYS, AND LOVE PLAYS BACK.
teach.b: God plays, and love plays back.

how: On Holi morning many Hindus greet elders first with a touch of gulal and a bow, then play with colored powder and water with family, friends and neighbors, sharing sweets like gujiya; in Braj, where the colors recall Krishna and Radha, the celebrations run for days.

s: the colors of Holi come from the Prahlada story
the fire remembers Prahlada. the colors are told through Krishna and Radha, a story families and songs tell.
on Holi, it's good form to greet elders first
a pinch of color on the feet or cheek, and a bow, before the play begins.
Krishna's play is just a kids' story, not Hindu teaching
lila, God's play, is a real Hindu idea. in Braj, Krishna plays with those who love him, and Holi joins the game.

games.q: you're young Krishna. you're upset that Radha is fair and you're dark, and you ask Yashoda why. what does she tell you?
o: go and put some color on her face.
wash your face in the river.
games.why: she laughs and says go and color her face, then. he does, and Radha colors him back. that, people say, is how the game began: lila, God at play.

practice: Picture a temple courtyard in Braj on Holi morning, petals and pink powder in the air. If you pray, say Radhe Radhe, the greeting heard all over Braj, and put a pinch of color at Krishna's feet first.
If you don't, picture someone you've drifted from: say happy Holi first, wait for the smile, a small pinch of pink on their cheek, and let them color you right back.

wordCard.voice: Holi. The spring festival: the fire the night before, for Prahlada, and the colors in the morning, for Krishna and Radha.

orig.note: Hindi; often linked to Holika, the demon king's sister who burned in the fire the night before.

carryVoice: Your line: lila. God plays, and love plays back. Tomorrow, nine nights begin. Day one hundred forty-two, done.
